geometryChanges: 43 main-hall bracket assemblies now use closed curved, bevelled, half-lapped timber profiles and pierced gilt end fittings. Pagoda uses its retained kit.
489 main/lower-roof rafters are continuous closed sweeps following the real roof surface. The former straight segmented rafter tips no longer run through the ceramic edge.
Upper-storey receiving beams and bracket seats are fitted between real beam tops and rafter undersides; repeated unsupported bracket strips were removed.
Lotus petals have separate front/back curved faces joined by a thin rolled rim, rounded ovate outlines, geometric fine pleats and individual opening variation.

Lotus leaves have closed upper/lower faces, a depressed centre, local edge curl, uneven radial folds and 19 raised primary veins. Petioles attach to the transformed lower-face centre with radius capped at 13 mm.
The near closed bud is a smooth capped five-lobed ovoid rather than the prior short straight lathe profile.
scopePreserved: Original site placement and low pond camera
Main roof ceramic body and gable silhouette
Bridge, pagoda, curtains, stairs, lanterns, trees and background lighting
materialInputs: Retained CC0 local timber scan. Botanical pigments/venation are procedural. Reference photograph is only a comparison input.
remainingDifferences: Overall roof volume, gable surface and reference silhouette remain materially different; this pass focused on the bearing/rafter kit.
Main hall brackets are continuous solids, but the cadence, carving detail and repeated broad faces still appear too regular and synthetic.
The flower and leaf are genuinely curved closed meshes, but petals, stamens, pigment variation and leaf cuticle remain too simplified and synthetic.
Pond reflection stretches into horizontal bands in the offset botanical subfrustum. It does not establish water/lens acceptance.
Native daylight, granite and foreground depth-of-field remain visibly different from the photograph.
copyright: Original reference photograph copyright retained by its owner; comparison only. No photograph is mapped onto a scene surface.
